introduction-the-shared-drive-problem.core: Many applications need a shared filesystem that several servers mount at once: content management, home directories, ML datasets, legacy Windows apps. EBS is single-instance and S3 isn't a filesystem, so AWS offers managed file services: EFS (NFS for Linux) and the FSx family (Windows, Lustre, NetApp ONTAP, OpenZFS).

first_principles.problem: A fleet of web servers needs the same uploaded files, and copying them around breaks consistency.
truths: Block volumes attach to one instance.
Different ecosystems need different protocols (NFS, SMB).

analogy.title: A shared network drive at the office
analogy.story: Everyone sees the same folders, but you choose the drive type that fits your team's computers and workload.
analogy.breaks: Office drives sit in one room; managed file systems replicate across AZs.

example.title: Picking a file service
flow: Linux web servers, elastic size → EFS
Windows app needing AD + SMB → FSx Windows

check.q: Why not use S3 as a shared filesystem for a legacy app?
check.a: S3 lacks POSIX semantics like file locking, renames and partial writes that many apps expect.

amazon-efs-the-linux-standard.core: EFS is a fully managed, elastic NFSv4.1 filesystem for Linux that grows and shrinks automatically, is accessible from many instances, containers and Lambda across AZs, and offers storage classes (Standard, IA, Archive) with lifecycle management. Throughput modes are Elastic (default), Provisioned or Bursting.

first_principles.problem: Containers across AZs need shared, persistent storage without capacity planning.
truths: NFS is the Linux standard for shared files.
Latency is higher than local disk.
derivation: **Access points** for per-app roots and POSIX identities.

analogy.title: A cloud-hosted shared folder that expands like a balloon
analogy.story: It grows as you add files and shrinks as you delete them.
analogy.breaks: Balloons have limits; EFS scales to petabytes.

example.title: Mount EFS

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: All web servers see the same uploads.

code.text:
sudo yum install -y amazon-efs-utils
sudo mount -t efs -o tls fs-0abc123:/ /mnt/shared

example.outcome: shared Linux storage with no capacity planning.

check.q: What is an EFS access point?
check.a: An application-specific entry point that enforces a root directory and POSIX user/group identity.

fsx-for-windows-file-server-the-corporat.core: FSx for Windows File Server provides fully managed native Windows file shares over SMB, integrated with Active Directory for permissions (NTFS ACLs), with DFS namespaces, shadow copies, deduplication and Multi-AZ deployment. It suits lifting Windows workloads and user shares to AWS.

first_principles.problem: A company moving to AWS needs its Windows 'S: drive' with AD permissions intact.
truths: Windows apps expect SMB and NTFS ACLs.
Managing Windows file servers is toil.
derivation: Join to **AWS Managed AD** or self-managed AD.
Use **SSD or HDD** storage by workload.

analogy.title: The office file server, minus the server cupboard
analogy.story: Same drive letters and permissions; someone else patches it.
analogy.breaks: The old server sat on the LAN; FSx is reached over VPN/Direct Connect from offices.

example.title: Migrating a department share
flow: Create Multi-AZ FSx joined to corp AD
example.outcome: Windows shares without servers to manage.

check.q: Why choose FSx for Windows over EFS for Windows apps?
check.a: EFS is NFS for Linux; Windows apps need SMB with NTFS ACLs and AD integration.

fsx-for-lustre-the-speed-demon.core: FSx for Lustre is a managed parallel filesystem delivering hundreds of GB/s and millions of IOPS with sub-ms latency for HPC and ML. It links to S3 buckets, lazily loading objects as files and exporting results back. Scratch deployments are cheapest for temporary jobs; persistent ones replicate within an AZ.

first_principles.problem: GPU training jobs stall reading millions of files from S3.
truths: S3 is durable but not POSIX-fast.
derivation: Choose **scratch** for short jobs, **persistent** for longer.

analogy.title: A pit lane fuel rig fed from the main tank
analogy.story: S3 is the big tank; Lustre delivers fuel at race speed to the cars.
analogy.breaks: Fuel is consumed; data is reused across epochs, so caching pays.

example.title: ML training setup
flow: FSx Lustre scratch linked to bucket

check.q: What does linking FSx for Lustre to S3 provide?
check.a: S3 objects appear as files and are loaded on first access, with results exportable back to S3.

fsx-for-netapp-ontap-the-enterprise-swis.core: FSx for NetApp ONTAP runs NetApp's ONTAP as a managed service: multi-protocol (NFS, SMB, iSCSI, NVMe/TCP), instant snapshots and clones, SnapMirror replication, deduplication/compression and automatic tiering to cheaper capacity storage. It's ideal for migrating existing NetApp estates or needing many protocols on one system.

first_principles.problem: An enterprise relies on NetApp features like SnapMirror and FlexClone and won't re-platform.
truths: Enterprises have ONTAP workflows and tooling.
derivation: Serve **NFS + SMB + iSCSI** from one filesystem.

analogy.title: A Swiss Army knife
analogy.story: One tool with many blades for different jobs.
analogy.breaks: Swiss Army knives are simple; ONTAP needs storage-admin skills.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Realistic test data without copying 2 TB each time.

check.q: What makes FlexClone useful for dev/test?
check.a: It creates writable copies instantly that share unchanged blocks, using almost no extra space.

fsx-for-openzfs-the-developers-nfs.core: FSx for OpenZFS offers managed ZFS over NFS with very low latency (hundreds of microseconds), high IOPS, instant snapshots and clones, and compression. It's a strong fit for migrating Linux/ZFS workloads, build farms and latency-sensitive NFS apps that EFS is too slow for.

first_principles.problem: A CI build farm on EFS is slow because of many small-file metadata operations.
truths: ZFS offers snapshots, clones and checksums.
EFS optimises for elasticity over latency.

analogy.title: A fast local workshop versus a big shared warehouse
analogy.story: The workshop is quicker for lots of small tasks; the warehouse scales endlessly.
analogy.breaks: Workshops are local; OpenZFS is still network storage.

example.title: Moving a build cache
flow: npm/maven caches with millions of small files

check.q: When would you choose FSx for OpenZFS over EFS?
check.a: For latency-sensitive or small-file-heavy NFS workloads, or when migrating ZFS-based systems.
